headline: Mesh LLM pools your GPUs for distributed AI computing on iroh
summary: New Mesh LLM software allows users to combine their existing GPUs and memory into a single, OpenAI-compatible API, enabling larger models and private compute sharing.
details: Mesh LLM offers a decentralized approach to running large language models, moving away from traditional data center reliance. It pools the GPUs and memory already available across multiple machines, presenting them as a unified, OpenAI-compatible API.

This architecture allows users to run larger models without needing to purchase more powerful hardware. It also facilitates private compute sharing for teams, enabling agents and chat applications to leverage distributed resources.

The system can partition large models across several machines using a 'split mode'. This allows modest hardware to collectively run models that would otherwise be too large for any single machine, with the complexity hidden from the end-user.

Under the hood, Mesh LLM utilizes iroh endpoints for secure, authenticated, and NAT-traversing QUIC connections between nodes. This peer-to-peer networking eliminates the need for central servers and simplifies connectivity.

The software is lightweight (around 18 MB) and can be installed to join a public mesh or configure private deployments. It exposes an OpenAI-compatible API at localhost:9337/v1, allowing standard clients to connect seamlessly.

Future plans include a mobile app built on iroh's Swift SDK, supporting the emerging ACP agent standard. The project's core philosophy emphasizes peer-to-peer interaction, reduced reliance on closed servers, and avoiding vendor lock-in.

headline_marked: [[Ask an LLM]] is the new 'I don't know,' author argues
headline: Ask an LLM is the new 'I don't know,' author argues
summary: As AI models become more prevalent, some users are opting to ask them instead of seeking human expertise, potentially losing valuable lived experience.
details: The author argues that the phrase 'ask Claude' has become a polite way to deflect difficult questions, similar to 'LMGTFY' in the past.
While many questions can be answered by AI or search engines, the author posits that questions which have already stumped LLMs require human insight and lived experience.
Seeking human advice for complex problems often yields more valuable answers than AI, as it taps into personal experience and nuanced understanding that models cannot replicate.
The article suggests that relying solely on LLMs for answers to challenging questions bypasses the opportunity to gain wisdom from human experts who have navigated similar issues.
This trend could devalue the expertise of individuals who are often sought out for their knowledge, as their insights are replaced by AI-generated responses.
